title: Ride Sharing Platform (Lyft / Grab): Complete Architecture
description: Design a global ride-hailing architecture with batched bipartite matchmaker dispatch, real-time map routing, surge pricing, and pooled rides.

data.text: Design a global on-demand ride-hailing platform like Lyft or Grab. The system coordinates millions of riders and drivers in real time across hundreds of cities. The central engineering challenge is the Dispatch Matchmaker: matching incoming ride requests to nearby drivers not merely on a greedy first-come basis, but through Batched Bipartite Matching in 5-second windows to maximize global network efficiency, minimize total rider ETA, minimize driver unpaid driving distance, calculate traffic-aware routing, and support dynamic shared rides (pooled rides).

terms.definition: Collecting ride requests and available drivers over a 5-second window, solving maximum-weight matching (Hungarian / Kuhn-Munkres algorithm) to optimize overall platform efficiency rather than greedy 1-to-1 dispatch.
A graph pre-processing speedup technique on road networks (OpenStreetMap) enabling sub-millisecond point-to-point shortest path and ETA calculations.
Dynamically matching two or more independent riders with overlapping route corridors into a single vehicle while enforcing strict detour time bounds.
Hierarchical spatial decomposition indexing moving driver GPS coordinates in memory for sub-millisecond radius search.
A resilient state machine driving the immutable ride lifecycle: REQUESTED -> MATCHED -> DRIVER_ARRIVED -> IN_TRIP -> COMPLETED -> SETTLED.

data.title: Functional Requirements
items: Rider Booking: Request standard or pooled rides with upfront fare estimates and pickup/drop-off route preview
Driver Fleet: Online/offline toggle, accept/decline ride dispatches, and in-app turn-by-turn navigation
Batch Matchmaker: Match batches of riders and drivers in rolling 5-second windows using bipartite graph optimization
Dynamic Pricing (Surge): Adjust fares dynamically per geospatial tile based on local real-time supply vs demand
Live Tracking: Stream real-time driver coordinates and live vehicle heading angle to rider maps every 3 seconds
Trip Settlement: Compute final fares, toll charges, driver split, and process payment upon ride completion

data.title: Non-Functional Requirements
items: Scale: 20M+ daily completed trips; 500,000 active concurrent drivers; 150,000 location pings/sec
Dispatch Match Latency: Dispatch decision returned to rider within 5-10 seconds of request submission
Routing Latency: <15ms P99 latency for point-to-point ETA and turn-by-turn path generation
Driver Location Freshness: Vehicle location on rider phone updated with <3 seconds end-to-end lag
High Availability: 99.999% uptime for core location tracking and active trip state machines

data.text: The platform separates high-frequency location telemetry from transactional trip coordination and batched matchmaker dispatching.

data.text: Unlike naive systems that dispatch the first driver who appears, the Batched Matchmaker gathers all requests in an H3 hexagonal cell over a 5-second window to find the globally optimal assignment.

faqs.question: Why is Batched Bipartite Matching superior to Greedy Dispatch?
faqs.answer: Greedy matching pairs Rider 1 with Driver 1 (1 min away). But 2 seconds later, Rider 2 requests a ride right next to Driver 1, but must now be assigned Driver 2 who is 15 minutes away! Cumulative wait time: 1 + 15 = 16 mins. In batched matching, a 5-second delay pairs Rider 1 with Driver 2 (4 mins) and Rider 2 with Driver 1 (2 mins). Total cumulative wait time: 6 mins, reducing cancellations and fuel waste across the city.

faqs.question: How are routing and ETAs computed in sub-15ms without querying external Google Maps APIs?
faqs.answer: Commercial map APIs charge per call and introduce 100ms+ network latency. Ride-sharing companies self-host OSRM (Open Source Routing Machine) or Valhalla instances using Contraction Hierarchies over OpenStreetMap data. Pre-contracting the road network reduces shortest path searches (Dijkstra) to sub-millisecond bidirectional graph traversals in memory.

faqs.question: How do Pooled / Shared rides calculate detours dynamically?
faqs.answer: Shared rides solve the Pickup and Delivery Problem with Time Windows (PDPTW). When Rider 2 requests a ride, the matchmaker checks active vehicles heading in the same direction. It simulates inserting Rider 2's pickup and drop-off into Driver 1's route. The match is only accepted if it adds no more than a hard threshold (e.g. max 5-8 minutes) to Rider 1's original estimated arrival.

faqs.question: How are driver GPS telemetry pings ingested without overwhelming databases?
faqs.answer: Drivers transmit GPS updates over UDP or lightweight persistent TCP sockets to Netty gateways. Updates do not touch relational databases; they write directly into an in-memory spatial index (Redis GEO) with a 5-second TTL and publish to Kafka. Cassandra records historical location trails asynchronously for safety dispute audits.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: 5-second batched bipartite matching maximizes global fleet efficiency and cuts rider wait times
Self-hosted routing engines with Contraction Hierarchies calculate ETAs in under 15ms in memory
Redis GEO and in-memory QuadTrees store active driver locations with lightweight 5-second leases
Trip Finite State Machines coordinate atomic state changes across rider and driver apps
Pooled rides evaluate route insertion permutations to guarantee strict detour time ceilings
data.takeaway: Scalable ride-sharing platforms achieve peak urban transit efficiency by replacing greedy dispatching with batched bipartite graph optimization and sub-millisecond in-memory routing.
